newsitem.title: GERMANY: German utililties plan to fight tax on reserves.
newsitem.headline: German utililties plan to fight tax on reserves.

text.p: German utility companies said on Monday they would fight the possible introduction of new taxes on their hidden reserves.

Following a report that state finance ministers will meet to discuss a proposal to tax the reserves, RWE AG and Viag AG's Bayernwerk told Reuters that they thought the legislation as it currently stood was correct.

A report in Monday's edition of the Spiegel news magazine said German utilities could end up paying between 1.5 billion marks ($889.8 million) and three billion marks in taxes on an estimated 45 billion marks in reserves to pay for mothballing nuclear plants.
The finance ministers are due to meet on Thursday to make a decision on whether or not they will introduce the tax.
"If there is a decision to introduce a tax, then we will fight it in the courts," a spokesman for RWE said.
The finance ministry in Bonn said that the decision involved tax liabilities for around seven billion marks that the companes put in reserve for operating costs of a nuclear waste dump in Gorleben.

The RWE spokesman said that it could in no way tolerate paying tax on its reserves for the Gorleben plant and said that the argument about taxing utility company's hidden reserves came up every time the public purse was empty.
The government spokeswoman said the tax liability would not affect the entire sum, but rather only the interest earned on the amount, but would not be drawn on how much was to be paid.
A spokesman for Bayernwerk said that the reserves were put aside based on current costs for junking nuclear plants and waste disposal costs.

The reserves were invested in such a way that the dividends and revenues from the investments would cover future costs of scrapping nuclear plants and covering waste disposal costs. Therefore the earnings had to remain tax-free, the Bayernwerk spokesman said.
Veba AG said it would wait and see what happened at the meeting before making any announcement. "Until the decision is made, we are making no comment," said a spokeswoman.
According to its annual report, RWE had reserves of 8.3 billion marks for "waste disposal in the nuclear energy sector" in the year to the end of 1995.
RWE had 15.5 billion marks set aside for the purpose in 1995/96 and Veba had 10.5 billion marks in reserves for the purpose in 1996.
